introduction_markdown:
**Cameroon General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. History 3 (0760), Paper 3 - Africa and World History, ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2024. Duration: three hours.**

Instructions to candidates: Candidates are required to answer FOUR questions, choosing ONE from each of the four sections (Section A: Africa, 1800-1945; Section B: Africa, 1945 to the present; Section C: World Revolutions and Diplomacy, 1700-1919; Section D: World, 1919 to the present date). All questions carry equal marks (25 marks each).

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.
incertitudes: Règle de choix : le sujet impose « answer FOUR questions, choosing ONE from each of the four sections ». `regles_choix` porte une règle « 1 sur 3 » par section (A, B, C, D), ce qui correspond exactement à la consigne imprimée ; la consigne complète est recopiée dans `introduction_markdown`.

Points : chaque question porte 25 marks imprimés (« All questions carry equal marks »), soit 100 points pour les quatre questions à traiter. Aucun écart de points constaté ; `points` vaut 25 pour l'exercice et pour l'unique question de chaque fichier.

Sujet scanné de deux pages (page de garde et questions 1 à 12) ; filigranes gcerevision ignorés. Défauts d'impression : le texte de la page 2 transparaît en miroir, très pâle, sur la page de garde (verso mal opacifié) et des traînées d'encre parasites encadrent les barèmes et les numéros (questions 2, 4, 7 et 8 notamment) sans gêner la lecture ; aucune question coupée ni illisible, aucune carte ni aucun document dans le sujet, donc aucune figure.

Aucun corrigé officiel : les corrigés sont des réponses modèles rédigées au niveau Advanced Level (introduction, développement, conclusion argumentée). Aucune citation n'est inventée et les chiffres sont limités à des repères datés de l'historiographie courante ; à relire par un historien avant mise en vente.

Thèmes : noms qualifiés, réutilisés des sujets History 2020-2024 déjà transcrits (`christian missionary activity in west africa`, `scramble for africa`, `indirect rule and assimilation`, `impact of world war two on africa`, `african independence movements`, `apartheid in south africa`, `glorious revolution of 1688`, `congress system after 1815`, `causes of world war one`, `league of nations`, `cold war`, `arab-israeli conflict`) ; deux noms nouveaux (`decolonisation of french west africa`, `berlin blockade and airlift`) sont qualifiés pour éviter une collision avec les Tags de l'Histoire francophone ; à revérifier à l'ingestion avec `find_tag_variant`.

Question 1 : les dates et institutions citées (CMS à Freetown, Fourah Bay College en 1827, Crowther évêque en 1864, mission de Calabar à partir de 1846, Native Baptist Church de 1888 au Cameroun, Niger Expedition de 1841) suivent l'historiographie courante ; aucun effectif de convertis ou d'élèves n'est avancé.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Discuss the significance of Christian missionary activities in West Africa in the 19th century.

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** Christian missionary activity in West Africa grew from the late eighteenth century and became a major force in the nineteenth. The Church Missionary Society (CMS), the Methodist (Wesleyan) mission, the Basel Mission, the Bremen (North German) Mission, the Church of Scotland and the Baptist Missionary Society, followed by Catholic orders such as the Holy Ghost Fathers and the Society of African Missions, worked from bases such as Freetown, Cape Coast, Accra, Abeokuta, Calabar and, in Cameroon, Douala and Victoria. To discuss their significance is to weigh what they achieved, what they damaged and how far they shaped the later history of the region. It can be argued that their influence was very great and lasting, above all in education, language, health and the emergence of a new African elite, but that it was also double-edged because they were closely tied to European expansion.

**1. Why the missionaries came.** The main motives were religious (the duty to convert Africans), humanitarian (the campaign against the Atlantic slave trade, which Britain abolished in 1807, and the wish to replace it by "legitimate commerce" and the "Bible and the plough" in the language of T. F. Buxton), and the evangelical revival in Europe. Freed captives settled at Freetown and later returned to Yorubaland provided the first converts and agents.

**2. Educational significance.**
- Missionaries opened the first schools. The CMS founded Fourah Bay College at Freetown in 1827, which became the main centre of higher education in British West Africa; later secondary schools included the CMS Grammar Schools in Freetown (1845) and Lagos (1859), the Methodist Boys' High School in Lagos (1878) and, in the Gold Coast, the Basel Mission and Wesleyan schools.
- Technical and teacher training were offered at places such as Calabar and Abeokuta, and in Cameroon the Baptist and later the Basel and Presbyterian missions ran schools on the coast and in the interior.
- Mission schools produced most of the first educated Africans: teachers, clergymen, clerks, interpreters, doctors and journalists. Many later became leaders of the nationalist movements of the twentieth century, so that the schools had a political significance which the missionaries did not intend.

**3. Language, culture and communication.** Missionaries reduced many African languages to writing and produced grammars, dictionaries, hymn books and Bible translations: Yoruba, Igbo and Efik, Twi and Ga, Ewe, and Duala in Cameroon (Alfred Saker). Samuel Ajayi Crowther, a liberated Yoruba captive, played a leading part in Yoruba and Igbo translation. Printing presses and early newspapers followed. This preserved vernacular languages and began a written literature.

**4. Health, welfare and humanitarian work.** Mission dispensaries, hospitals and leprosy centres introduced Western medicine, and mission stations sheltered freed slaves, orphans and the rejected. Missionaries such as Mary Slessor at Calabar (from 1876) campaigned against the killing of twins and human sacrifice, and Alfred Saker founded Victoria in 1858 as a settlement for freed slaves and converts. Missionaries also encouraged new crops, skills and "legitimate commerce".

**5. Religious and political significance.**
- Christianity spread most widely in the coastal and forest zones, and the Church gradually acquired African leadership. Crowther was consecrated the first African Anglican bishop in 1864, on the principle of a self-governing African church supported by Henry Venn of the CMS.
- When European missionaries began to replace African clergy in the 1880s and 1890s, Africans formed independent churches, such as the United Native African Church in Lagos (1891) and the Native Baptist Church in Cameroon (1888) after the Baptist mission passed to German missionaries.
- Missionaries sometimes opened the way for European rule: they acted as interpreters, informants and intermediaries, advised on treaties, and called for protection (for example at Abeokuta and, in Cameroon, in the request to Britain by Duala chiefs to annex the coast before Germany took it in 1884). Their schools usually taught respect for the new authorities.

**6. Limitations and criticisms.** Missionaries often condemned African religion, polygamy, secret societies and dances as pagan and demanded a complete break with them, which divided families and communities. Denominational rivalry wasted resources. Education was mostly literary and clerical rather than technical, and the Muslim north of West Africa was largely closed to the missions. Mission work was also held back by disease (the Niger Expedition of 1841 lost many Europeans to fever) and shortage of funds.

**7. Assessment.** Their significance was therefore both constructive and ambiguous. In the long run the schools, written languages, hospitals and the emergence of African churches had permanent effects on West African society, and the educated elite they created was central to the later struggle for independence. At the same time, the missions contributed to cultural disruption and, indirectly, to colonial penetration.

**Conclusion.** Christian missionary activities were of great significance in nineteenth century West Africa: they introduced Western education, medicine and literacy, helped to end the slave trade and encouraged a new kind of society and leadership, even though their cultural intolerance and their link with imperial expansion damaged their moral authority and provoked African reactions which shaped the modern religious and political life of the region.
